◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Computers can't store most real numbers exactly, so every numerical answer carries error. Knowing the sources and size of that error is what separates a trustworthy computation from garbage.

Error types
Absolute error = |true − approx|. Relative error = |true − approx| / |true|. Round-off error comes from finite floating-point precision; truncation error comes from cutting off an infinite process (a series, a limit).
WORKED EXAMPLE — absolute vs relative error

Approximating π ≈ 3.14 (true 3.14159...):

Absolute error ≈ 0.00159. Relative error ≈ 0.00159 / 3.14159 ≈ 0.0005 = 0.05%.

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Absolute error alone is misleading across scales — an error of 1 is huge for a quantity of 2 but tiny for a quantity of 10⁹. Relative error is usually what matters.

📊 FIGURE — Floating-point numbers are NOT evenly spaced
Floats crowd densely near zero and spread out as magnitude grows — the gap between neighbors doubles at each power of two. Relative precision stays constant (~16 digits in double), but ABSOLUTE gaps grow: at 10¹⁶ the next float is a whole integer away.
📊 FIGURE — why exact arithmetic and machine arithmetic disagree
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Why 0.1 + 0.2 is not 0.3

A tenth is a repeating fraction in binary, exactly as a third is in decimal. The stored double nearest 0.1 is a little above it, the one nearest 0.2 a little below, and their sum is not the stored double nearest 0.3.

Printed to 20 decimal places:

  • 0.1 + 0.2 = 0.30000000000000004441
  • 0.3 = 0.29999999999999998890
  • difference ≈ 5.55 × 10⁻¹⁷

The moral is not that floating point is broken — it is that equality is the wrong test. Compare with a tolerance: |a − b| < ε.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Curing cancellation with the conjugate

Computing √(x + 1) − √x for large x subtracts two nearly equal numbers, so the leading digits cancel and what survives is mostly rounding error. Multiply above and below by the conjugate:

√(x+1) − √x = [(x+1) − x] / [√(x+1) + √x] = 1 / (√(x+1) + √x)

The rewritten form adds, so nothing cancels. At x = 10¹⁶ the direct formula returns exactly 0 in double precision — every significant digit is gone — while the conjugate form returns 5 × 10⁻⁹, which is correct.

The two expressions are algebraically identical and numerically worlds apart. That gap is what numerical analysis is about.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Reading 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3 as a bug in the language. Every IEEE-754 system behaves this way, because the three values have no exact finite binary representation. Test floating-point equality with a tolerance, never with ==.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Bisection is the simplest, most reliable root-finder: if a continuous function changes sign across an interval, a root is trapped inside, and halving the interval corners it. Slow but guaranteed.

Bisection
To solve f(x)=0 on [a,b] with f(a)·f(b) < 0: compute the midpoint m; keep the half where the sign change persists; repeat. The interval halves each step, so error ≤ (b−a)/2ⁿ after n steps.
WORKED EXAMPLE — one bisection step

f(x) = x² − 2 on [1, 2]: f(1) = −1 < 0, f(2) = 2 > 0, so a root (√2) is inside.

Midpoint m = 1.5: f(1.5) = 0.25 > 0. Sign change is now on [1, 1.5], so keep that half. Continue to squeeze toward √2 ≈ 1.414.

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Bisection requires an initial bracket where f changes sign, f(a)·f(b) < 0. It cannot find roots where the function only touches the axis (double roots) without crossing.

📊 FIGURE — Bisection: keep the half that still brackets the root
f(a) < 0 and f(b) > 0, so a root hides between them. Test the midpoint: f(m) > 0 here, so the root lies in [a, m] — throw the right half away. Every step halves the interval; slow but absolutely guaranteed.
📊 FIGURE — what bisection needs and what it guarantees
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — How many steps for a given tolerance

Starting from a bracket of width 1, after n bisections the interval has width 1/2ⁿ. To guarantee an error below 10⁻³ you need

1/2ⁿ < 10⁻³  ⟺  2ⁿ > 1000

2⁹ = 512, which is not enough; 2¹⁰ = 1024, which is. So 10 steps — roughly three correct decimal digits.

The rule of thumb worth memorising: about 10 bisections per 3 decimal digits, because 2¹⁰ ≈ 10³.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Choosing a valid starting bracket

For f(x) = x³ − 4 the requirement is f(a)·f(b) < 0. Evaluate:

  • f(0) = −4, f(1) = −3 → both negative, [0, 1] is not a bracket
  • f(1) = −3, f(2) = 4 → signs differ, [1, 2] works
  • f(2) = 4, f(3) = 23 → both positive, [2, 3] is not a bracket

The root is ∛4 ≈ 1.5874, which indeed lies in [1, 2].

Note what a sign change does not tell you: that there is exactly one root. It guarantees at least one; an interval with two roots may show no sign change at all.

🎯 EXAM TIP
Bisection is the method that always works and always works slowly. It needs only continuity and a sign change — no derivative — and it cannot diverge. The cost is linear convergence: one extra bit of accuracy per step, versus Newton's doubling of correct digits.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Newton's method uses the derivative to leap toward a root, doubling the number of correct digits each step (quadratic convergence) — the go-to fast root-finder when it works.

Newton's iteration
x_{n+1} = x_n − f(x_n)/f'(x_n). Geometrically: follow the tangent line to where it crosses the axis, and repeat. Convergence is quadratic near a simple root.
WORKED EXAMPLE — one Newton step

Solve x² − 2 = 0 from x₀ = 1.5. f(x) = x²−2, f'(x) = 2x.

x₁ = 1.5 − (1.5² − 2)/(2·1.5) = 1.5 − 0.25/3 ≈ 1.4167. Already close to √2 ≈ 1.41421 — one step, three correct digits.

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Newton can DIVERGE or cycle if the guess is poor, and it fails where f'(x) ≈ 0 (division by near-zero flings the iterate away). Unlike bisection, convergence isn't guaranteed.

📊 FIGURE — Newton’s method: ride the tangent to the axis
From the guess x₀, climb to the curve, draw the tangent, and follow it down to the axis: that crossing is x₁ — usually dramatically closer to the root. Repeat and the correct digits roughly double each round (quadratic convergence).
📊 FIGURE — Newton's iteration and its fine print
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — One Newton step on cos x − x

With f(x) = cos x − x and x₀ = 1 radian:

  • f(1) = cos 1 − 1 = 0.5403 − 1 = −0.4597
  • f′(x) = −sin x − 1, so f′(1) = −0.8415 − 1 = −1.8415
  • x₁ = 1 − (−0.4597)/(−1.8415) = 1 − 0.2496 = 0.7504

The true root is 0.7391, so one step has taken the error from 0.26 to 0.011.

Watch the signs: both f and f′ are negative here, so the quotient is positive and gets subtracted. Using +f/f′ by mistake gives 1.2496 — moving away from the root.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Newton on x² − a is the Babylonian method

Substituting f(x) = x² − a and f′(x) = 2x into the iteration:

xₙ₊₁ = xₙ − (xₙ² − a)/(2xₙ) = (2xₙ² − xₙ² + a)/(2xₙ) = (xₙ + a/xₙ)/2

That is the ancient Babylonian square-root algorithm: average your guess with a/guess. For a = 2 from x₀ = 1: 1.5, 1.416667, 1.4142157, 1.4142136 — correct to 8 digits in four steps, the digits doubling each time.

Contrast f(x) = (x − 2)², which has a double root at 2. There f′(2) = 0, the quadratic guarantee fails, and Newton merely halves the error each step — linear convergence.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Assuming Newton always beats bisection. It converges quadratically only near a simple root. If f′(xₙ) is near zero the step is enormous and the iteration can fly off entirely; at a double root it degrades to linear; and from a poor starting point it may cycle or diverge. Bisection is slower but cannot fail.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Interpolation builds a smooth function passing exactly through data points — filling gaps, building tables, and underpinning numerical integration and differentiation.

Interpolation
Through n+1 points there is a UNIQUE polynomial of degree ≤ n. The Lagrange form writes it as a weighted sum of basis polynomials, each 1 at one node and 0 at the others.
WORKED EXAMPLE — linear interpolation

Estimate f(2.5) given f(2) = 4 and f(3) = 9 (linear interp).

f(2.5) ≈ 4 + (9−4)·(2.5−2)/(3−2) = 4 + 5·0.5 = 6.5. (The true x² value is 6.25 — interpolation error.)

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Higher-degree interpolation isn't always better: with many equally-spaced points, the polynomial can oscillate wildly near the ends (Runge's phenomenon). Splines avoid this.

📊 FIGURE — Runge’s phenomenon — and the Chebyshev cure
Fitting one high-degree polynomial through EQUALLY spaced points goes wild at the edges (red). Clustering the nodes toward the endpoints (Chebyshev spacing, green ticks) tames the oscillation — or sidestep it entirely with piecewise splines.
"}, "NUMER/ch2/s2": {"body": "
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Most integrals have no closed form. Quadrature rules approximate ∫f by sampling f at points — the trapezoidal rule uses straight-line pieces, Simpson's uses parabolas for much better accuracy.

Trapezoidal & Simpson
Trapezoidal (n intervals, width h): ∫ ≈ (h/2)[f₀ + 2f₁ + ... + 2f_{n−1} + f_n]. Simpson's (n even): ∫ ≈ (h/3)[f₀ + 4f₁ + 2f₂ + 4f₃ + ... + f_n]. Simpson's is exact for cubics.
WORKED EXAMPLE — trapezoidal rule

Approximate ∫₀² x² dx with one trapezoid (h = 2). f(0) = 0, f(2) = 4.

Trapezoid ≈ (2/2)(0 + 4) = 4. True value = 8/3 ≈ 2.67 — one trapezoid overestimates; more subintervals improve it.

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Simpson's rule needs an EVEN number of subintervals (it pairs them into parabolas). It's dramatically more accurate than trapezoidal for smooth functions — error ∝ h⁴ vs h².

📊 FIGURE — The trapezoid rule
Connect the sampled curve points with straight chords and add up the trapezoids beneath — a big accuracy upgrade over flat-topped rectangles at the same cost. Simpson’s rule goes one better, fitting a parabola through each pair of panels.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Derivatives from data or black-box functions use finite differences — the same idea as the difference quotient, but with a real (nonzero) step, forcing a delicate trade-off between two kinds of error.

Finite differences
Forward: f'(x) ≈ [f(x+h) − f(x)]/h (error ∝ h). Central: f'(x) ≈ [f(x+h) − f(x−h)]/(2h) (error ∝ h², more accurate).
WORKED EXAMPLE — central difference

Estimate f'(1) for f(x) = x², h = 0.1, using central difference.

[f(1.1) − f(0.9)]/(0.2) = [1.21 − 0.81]/0.2 = 0.40/0.2 = 2.0 — exactly f'(1) = 2 (central difference is exact for quadratics).

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Shrinking h reduces TRUNCATION error but eventually AMPLIFIES round-off (subtracting nearly-equal numbers, divided by a tiny h). There's an optimal h — smaller isn't always better.

📊 FIGURE — The derivative: secant lines becoming the tangent
The dashed secant joins two points on the curve — its slope is the average rate (f(a+h) − f(a))/h. As h shrinks, the second point slides into the first and the secant tips into the solid tangent line: its slope is the derivative f′(a), the instantaneous rate.
📊 FIGURE — why the two operations behave oppositely
🎯 EXAM TIP
Compared with numerical integration, numerical differentiation is more sensitive to noise. Integration averages errors away; differentiation subtracts nearby values (cancellation) and then divides by a small h, magnifying what is left. This is why shrinking h does not keep helping — truncation error falls but rounding error rises, so the total error has a minimum at some moderate h.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Solving Ax = b is the most common task in scientific computing (it hides inside regression, simulation, and graphics). Gaussian elimination and its LU factorization are the standard workhorses.

Gaussian elimination & LU
Row-reduce [A|b] to upper-triangular, then back-substitute. LU factorization writes A = LU (lower × upper), so many systems with the same A are solved cheaply. Partial PIVOTING (swapping in the largest pivot) controls round-off.
WORKED EXAMPLE — back substitution

After elimination: 2x + y = 5 and 3y = 9. From the second, y = 3.

Substitute back: 2x + 3 = 5 ⇒ x = 1. Solution (x,y) = (1,3).

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Without pivoting, a tiny pivot element magnifies round-off catastrophically. ALWAYS use partial pivoting (swap rows to put the largest available entry on the diagonal) for numerical stability.

📊 FIGURE — One row operation, one step toward triangular
Gaussian elimination clears entries below each pivot with row operations. Here R₂ ← R₂ − 2R₁ kills the 2 under the first pivot, leaving an upper-triangular system you can finish by back-substitution: −y = −2 gives y = 2, then x = 5 − 2·2 = 1.
"}, "NUMER/ch3/s2": {"body": "
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

For huge, SPARSE systems (millions of unknowns, mostly zeros), direct elimination is too costly. Iterative methods refine a guess repeatedly and exploit sparsity.

Jacobi & Gauss–Seidel
Both solve each equation for its diagonal variable and iterate. Jacobi uses all OLD values per sweep; Gauss–Seidel uses the freshest values immediately (usually faster). Convergence is guaranteed when A is diagonally dominant.
WORKED EXAMPLE — when to iterate

A finite-difference grid of a PDE gives a system where each unknown couples to only its neighbors — mostly zeros.

Direct O(n³) elimination is wasteful; an iterative method touching only nonzeros converges far more cheaply.

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Iterative methods aren't guaranteed to converge for every matrix. Diagonal dominance (each diagonal entry larger in magnitude than the rest of its row) is the classic sufficient condition.

📊 FIGURE — Iterative solves: each sweep gets closer
Starting from a guess, every Jacobi or Gauss–Seidel sweep moves the estimate toward the true solution; with a well-conditioned (e.g. diagonally dominant) matrix the error shrinks by a steady factor — linear convergence you can watch happen.
📊 FIGURE — stopping an iteration you could run forever
🎯 EXAM TIP
Iterative methods produce successively better approximations, so you stop on a measured criterion: the step ‖x⁽ᵏ⁺¹⁾ − x⁽ᵏ⁾‖ or the residual ‖b − Ax⁽ᵏ⁾‖ falling below a tolerance. The residual is the more trustworthy of the two — a tiny step can mean slow convergence rather than a solution, so a step test alone can stop a long way from the answer.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Simulating dynamics — orbits, circuits, populations — means solving ODEs numerically. Runge–Kutta (RK4) is the industry-standard: far more accurate than Euler for the same step size.

Euler vs RK4
Euler: y_{n+1} = y_n + h·f(t_n, y_n), first-order (error ∝ h). RK4 samples the slope four times per step and blends them, fourth-order (error ∝ h⁴) — vastly more accurate.
WORKED EXAMPLE — why RK4 wins

Halving the step size h reduces Euler's error by ~2× but RK4's error by ~16× (2⁴).

So RK4 achieves high accuracy with much larger steps, saving computation despite doing more work per step.

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

A method can be accurate yet UNSTABLE: for stiff equations, an explicit method blows up unless h is tiny. Stiff problems need implicit methods (e.g. backward Euler).

📊 FIGURE — Euler’s method: chasing a curve with straight steps
Start on the true solution (green) and repeatedly step along the CURRENT tangent slope for a width h. The polyline drifts from the curve — error builds each step — but shrinking h (or upgrading to RK4’s four slope samples) tightens the chase dramatically.
📊 FIGURE — what \"pth order\" buys you
🎯 EXAM TIP
Halving h reduces RK4's error by a factor of about 16, because the method is fourth order and 2⁴ = 16. The general rule is the one to carry: a pth-order method improves by 2ᵖ when you halve the step. That is also how you measure an unknown order — halve h, take the ratio of the errors, and read off log₂ of it.

Formulas & method

Root finding locates x with f(x)=0 by improving an estimate step by step.

Newton's method

x_{n+1} = x_n − f(x_n)/f'(x_n). Each step needs the function and its derivative at the current point.

Bisection

On a bracket [a,b] with a sign change, the midpoint is c = (a+b)/2. Keep the half where the sign change remains. After n steps the error is bounded by (b−a)/2ⁿ.

Secant method

x_{n+1} = x_n − f(x_n)·(x_n−x_{n−1}) / (f(x_n)−f(x_{n−1})) — like Newton but with a finite-difference slope.

Fixed-point iteration

Rewrite as x = g(x) and iterate x_{n+1} = g(x_n).

Error

Absolute error = |true − approx|; relative error = |true − approx| / |true|.

Worked example

Newton on f(x)=x²−2, f'(x)=2x, x₀=1: x₁ = 1 − (1−2)/(2·1) = 1 − (−0.5) = 1.5. One more step drives it toward √2 ≈ 1.4142.

"}, "NUMER/solving/sv2": {"body": "

Formulas & method

Linear interpolation

Through (x₀,y₀),(x₁,y₁): y = y₀ + (y₁−y₀)/(x₁−x₀)·(x−x₀).

Lagrange (quadratic)

P(x) = Σ yᵢ Lᵢ(x), each Lᵢ being the product of (x−xⱼ)/(xᵢ−xⱼ) over j≠i. For three points it reproduces the unique quadratic through them.

Trapezoidal rule

With step h: ∫ ≈ h/2·(f₀ + 2f₁ + … + 2f_{n−1} + fₙ). Error bound ≤ (b−a)h²/12·max|f''|.

Simpson's rule

(n even): ∫ ≈ h/3·(f₀ + 4f₁ + 2f₂ + 4f₃ + … + fₙ) — pattern 1,4,2,4,…,4,1. Exact for cubics.

Forward-difference derivative

f'(x) ≈ (f(x+h) − f(x)) / h.

Condition number

For evaluating f: κ = |x·f'(x)/f(x)|.

Worked example

Trapezoid for ∫₀² x² dx with n=2 (h=1), values 0,1,4: h/2·(0 + 2·1 + 4) = ½·6 = 3, versus the exact 8/3 ≈ 2.667.

These tools estimate values, integrals and derivatives from sample points.

Linear interpolation

Between (x₀,y₀) and (x₁,y₁): y = y₀ + (y₁ − y₀)/(x₁ − x₀) · (x − x₀).

Lagrange interpolation

P(x) = Σ yᵢ Lᵢ(x), where each basis Lᵢ(x) is the product of (x − xⱼ)/(xᵢ − xⱼ) over j ≠ i. It passes through every data point exactly.

Simpson's rule

Error
